claims.text: In conventional, equilibrated high-entropy alloys, lattice distortion is the primary determinant of hardness and strength.
Lattice distortion in these alloys stems from atomic-size mismatch.
Adding a minor isoelectronic element with a substantially different atomic radius increases lattice strain.
The added element produces uniform lattice distortion throughout the HEA crystal lattice.
Lattice strain caused by atomic-size mismatch acts as a barrier to dislocation motion.
Greater resistance to dislocation motion elevates yield strength and hardness.
In homogenized HEAs, size-mismatch strengthening is dominant over strengthening associated with localized chemical ordering.
Increasing induced lattice distortion will systematically increase hardness relative to the baseline HEA.
Increasing induced lattice distortion will systematically increase strength relative to the baseline HEA.
The predicted trend is limited by the onset of phase instability or segregation.
A conventional HEA with minimal atomic-size mismatch has hardness and strength consistent with traditional solid-solution strengthening models.
The proposed comparison should use single-phase, thermally equilibrated HEAs under quasi-static, room-temperature testing.
Rapid, non-equilibrium processing can introduce strengthening behavior not governed primarily by atomic-size mismatch.
In multiphase HEAs, phase-related mechanisms can dominate mechanical strength.
X-ray diffraction can be used in the proposed experiment to quantify lattice distortion and atomic-size mismatch.
Failure of hardness and strength to increase systematically with measured atomic-size mismatch would falsify the hypothesis.
The quantitative contribution of lattice distortion relative to short-range chemical order is uncertain.
The atomic-size-disparity threshold at which phase stability is compromised is unknown.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis is explicitly limited to single-phase alloys and predicts the trend only up to the onset of phase instability, yet the falsification rule treats phase instability or segregation as a falsifying observation. Such an observation falls outside the stated validity domain rather than directly falsifying the in-domain mechanism.
